habitat: Extremely secretive in flooded grassland and small pools. It occasionally breeds in southern Africa in years of good rainfall.
summary: An uncommon summer visitor. Orange-buff undertail coverts and white lines on the mantle and wings. The female has blue-grey underparts and the male is rich buff. The identification line says the underparts are buffy-brown, which conflicts with that sex difference. The upper parts are dark brown with white feather edges, streaky rather than spotted. The bill is thicker and darker than Spotted Crake, which is not in this list. The night call is a ticking tak-tak-taktak-tak. Avibase marks it rare or accidental, and Newman does not name the months, so the months are unset. The Kemp name Striped Crake and the code NB were left unchanged.

similar.note: African Crake has boldly barred underparts, a pinkish bill and a red eye. Striped Crake has orange-buff undertail coverts and white lines on the mantle.

calls.description: A constant night ticking like a wristwatch, tak-tak-taktak-tak. Grade A call from Temba, Bojanala, North West, with another species in the background. The filename is XC355772-Striped Crake.mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it an uncommon summer visitor. Avibase marks the Kruger occurrence rare or accidental, and the months are not named, so status is summer-migrant and monthsPresent is unset. The female underparts are blue-grey and the male is rich buff, while the identification line says buffy-brown. No photograph that shows the plumage was found. The grade A call is from North West. Population figures and the Kemp code NB were left unchanged.
